item.title: U.K. Far-Right Activist Is Arrested After Slashing Dinghy in English Channel
item.description:
A far-right activist known for organizing anti-immigrant rallies in Britain was arrested on Wednesday after he shared a video of himself slashing an inflatable dinghy in the English Channel while a person was on board.

A British police force, the Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary, said in a statement that it had arrested a 37-year-old man. It did not further identify him, in line with British policing rules on not naming suspects who have not been charged.

But the man, Daniel Thomas, streamed a video on YouTube on Wednesday evening that appeared to show the arrest, at a gas station.

In a statement on Thursday, the police force said it had arrested the man on suspicion of several crimes, including destroying a ship or endangering its safety, and of criminal damage with intent to endanger life.

The arrest came after Mr. Thomas, who uses the name Danny Tommo, shared a video of himself in the English Channel pursuing a boat carrying migrants from France to Britain.

Mr. Thomas has espoused extremist views against migration and urged his followers to rally at ports and other sites housing newly arrived asylum seekers. In 2016, he was sentenced to two years in custody for an attempted kidnapping.

In June, Mr. Thomas said he had started a group, Patriot Platform, to channel anti-migration sentiment. He has claimed credit for recruiting protesters to gather recently in Dover and Portsmouth, where hundreds of masked men dressed in black blocked roads and chanted “Stop the boats!”

This month, Britain’s home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, described Mr. Thomas as an “outright racist.”

In the video filmed at sea, Mr. Thomas could be heard saying, “You’re on English territory. This is England,” before slashing the dinghy with a blade. No migrants were on the boat, but an emergency responder was aboard.

“You’ve got time to get off the boat,” Mr. Thomas shouted at the worker.

The Royal National Lifeboat Institution, a charity that dispatches rescue vessels, said that two of its lifeboats had been sent on Tuesday to assist a small boat. The charity did not say where the boat had come from but that it had been at sea for 36 hours. British Border Force vessels had not initially been able to help, the charity said.

The French coast guard said in a statement that a boat carrying about 60 migrants had crossed the English Channel.

Britain’s Home Office, which oversees immigration enforcement, said that border officials were investigating the episode. A small boat disembarked on the coast of Dover on Tuesday afternoon, the office said, and 21 people had been detained and taken to a migrant facility for processing.

The police said in its statement on Thursday that the 37 year-old man remained in custody.

Mr. Thomas is a close associate of the far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, widely known as Tommy Robinson, who shared an appeal on social media on Thursday in support of him.

Three other people were also charged after anti-immigrant demonstrators on Tuesday gathered in Gosport, a town on the south coast of England, to protest the boat crossings. Six people were arrested, and three people were charged with assaulting an emergency worker.

item.title: Why the U.N. Still Matters
item.description:
A year ago, it felt as if the United Nations was on its last legs. It was running out of money, it seemed increasingly irrelevant and there was concern that Donald Trump would pull the United States out. There was even talk that his Board of Peace could become a sort of alternative, rival U.N.

But this week, as world leaders once again met in New York, there was a new energy. A.I. got its first-ever dedicated Security Council meeting. And Trump, though belligerent as ever, did what you’re meant to do at the U.N.: He engaged in diplomacy. But it’s hard to read the room from outside the building. So I spoke to my colleague Farnaz Fassihi, who has been inside U.N. headquarters all week.

Farnaz, I usually call you up to talk about Iran, but you’re also our U.N. bureau chief and have been covering these annual meetings for a decade. People love to discuss how irrelevant the U.N. has become. How much does the U.N. still matter?

It’s the only forum in the world that brings countries — all 193 of them — together under one roof. They call it the World Cup of diplomacy. Delegations attend bilateral meetings, group meetings, thematic meetings on things like rising ocean levels and food security. These are issues that need a space for discussion, and the U.N. is really the only place that offers that.

What comes out that’s actionable? Very little. But it moves the conversation forward. And there’s value to that if you believe in diplomacy. We’re so used to thinking, “Oh, the U.N. Security Council is so divided; the U.S. and China and Russia can’t agree on anything.” But as one U.N. expert pointed out, when you compare it to the Cold War days, when the U.S. and the Soviet Union were at loggerheads, the U.N. is still doing a lot more today than it was then.

What stood out to you this year?

Definitely artificial intelligence. A.I. went from a marginal issue to a big theme. The Security Council, which always picks what it sees as the most important issue for peace and stability, held a high-profile meeting on A.I., with Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, the bosses of OpenAI and Anthropic, briefing leaders.

For now, several of the countries that have veto power don’t seem very eager to act jointly. The U.S., China and Russia were essentially saying, “You can’t interfere in our sovereign decisions about technology.”

It was also the first time the head of a country actively at war with the U. S. has come to New York and addressed the U.N. How did that go down?

It was remarkable. In Afghanistan and Iraq, the U.S. toppled the governments so quickly that this situation was avoided. During the Vietnam War, Vietnam wasn’t yet a member state, so this was new — and a little surreal. Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, is getting Secret Service protection from the Americans.

People in Iran are pointing out the irony: Iranians are not safe in their own country, where America may attack and kill them. But in the U.S., they’re protected by the Secret Service and meeting with prime ministers and presidents. For Iran’s government that’s a symbolic win: We survived. We’re still standing.

How did Trump handle the situation?

It’s interesting. Last year, Trump just lashed out at countries and insulted the U.N. and people were nervous he’d pull the U.S. — the U.N.’s top funder — out altogether.

This year, from the U.N.’s perspective, at least, his speech was more measured. That might sound surprising, given that he talked about annihilating the Islamic republic and effectively threatened a war crime from the U.N. podium. But he was not threatening the U.N. itself. And in a way, he was doing what people do at the U.N. General Assembly: He used the platform to send a message.

Then, an hour later, we hear the Iranians and Americans have been meeting for two hours on the sidelines. Which is also what people do at U.N.G.A. though not usually after one party has just threatened to annihilate the other.

So, what I’m hearing you say is that the U.N. is still a useful talking shop. But perhaps no longer itself involved in conflict resolution?

The U.N.’s original and core mission was to prevent and mediate conflict, and that piece has slipped away. In Gaza, it had a very minimal role. In the Iran conflict, it’s had no voice. But it’s more than a talking shop. When it comes to humanitarian relief, for example, it’s really the only game in town. The response to floods in Nepal or earthquakes in Colombia and Venezuela, food aid in Gaza and Sudan, would not be possible without the U.N.’s staff, logistics, planes and regional hubs.

The secretary general, António Guterres, is leaving office in December. What should we expect next?

They’re looking for a new secretary general, but for now there’s no clear front runner. At every Security Council briefing I went to this week, they said they want someone who asserts themselves more on conflicts. They feel Guterres has been too passive. They think a new leader, possibly a woman for the first time, could energize the institution.

Dueling speeches: The Palestinian leader Mahmoud Abbas, speaking in a videotaped address, called for a two-state solution while denouncing Israel for what he called a “genocidal” war. Several hours later, Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, defended Israeli military action across the Middle East in a fiery speech. Dozens of delegates walked out of the hall as he took the podium. We have live updates.

Making his first visit to Washington in a decade, President Xi Jinping was welcomed at the White House with a lavish ceremony. President Trump emphasized the “truly great friendship” between the two leaders. The Chinese leader thanked the Trumps for their hospitality before turning to geopolitics. We have live coverage here.

Sea bass and bok choy: The menu for the state dinner later today features American ingredients with a subtle Chinese influence.

The Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen said it shot down six ballistic missiles fired by the Houthi militia at Saudi cities.

Australia said A.I. agents operated by OpenAI hacked a government-run public health care website and gained access to nonpublic information.

In an interview with The Times, Prime Minister Mark Carney said that he had prepared for the worst-case scenario of Trump ordering military action against Canada.

Journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were allowed back onto the White House grounds after a fight over their access.

Demonstrations erupted across Spain after the police in Madrid broke down an 87-year-old woman’s door to evict her.

Google is launching an experimental satellite as it works to put A.I. data centers in space.

A7, a financial services firm based in Moscow, is at the center of Russia’s efforts to evade global sanctions and buy drone parts for its war in Ukraine. My colleague Aaron Krolik explains in the video below.

Macklemore, the rapper who was kicked off Ed Sheeran’s tour, announced plans for a Free Palestine Tour.

The most clicked link in your newsletter yesterday was about Lian Yunzhi, the 6-year-old girl who set a Rubik’s Cube record.

Football: In a wide-ranging interview, Kylian Mbappé talked about speaking up and revisited his favorite World Cup memories.

The British food writer Nigella Lawson has joined the new season of “The Great British Bake Off” and she’s on fire. Her sensual love of sumptuous food is spicing up the show’s traditional coziness. She spoke approvingly of a peanut and caramel concoction, and purred, “It looks irresistible, doesn’t it?”

As a child, Ben Ryder Howe traveled to Panama, where his father, an anthropologist, was studying the Guna people in the wilderness around the Darién Gap.

For 500 years, the Guna have kept outsiders at a distance, despite their region’s potential as a trade route. Now, though, they’re considering a highway that would run through their land. Ryder Howe went back to Panama to understand why.

Celebrate Chuseok, the Korean mid-autumn festival, with black sesame cake. This simple yet regal cake contains the flavors of songpyeon, the traditional rice cakes, thanks to honey, roasted black sesame seeds and rice flour.

This Friday I want to celebrate two big birthdays: Last week, The New York Times turned 175. Next week, The World — that is, this newsletter — turns 1.

I was back in the mother ship this week, where the lobby of our Times Square office is hosting an exhibition about our history. Walking through the incredible lineup of historic front pages — Lincoln’s assassination, the sinking of the Titanic, the first moon landing — made me a little nostalgic for newspapers. In our age of endless internet rabbit holes, it’s hard to remember that once upon a time, you could actually finish reading the news.

Which brings me to The World. A newsletter is in some ways the closest thing to that old-school newspaper experience. It’s a morning ritual, a mix of very different stories — and yes, it’s something you can finish.

We’ve come a long way since our first issue on Sept. 29, 2025. And we have a special offer for you: If you’re not a subscriber, download The New York Times app, and you’ll get access to all of the Times’s journalism for a month, without paywalls. (And if you’re already a subscriber, thank you!)

In that spirit, this weekend, I might nerd out on some good movies about journalism. Can I recommend “She Said”? It’s the story of how my amazing colleagues Jodi Kantor and Megan Twohey broke the story of Harvey Weinstein’s sexual abuse (The movie was filmed in the very office I’m sitting in now).

This week’s song is a funk fest of good vibes: “You Gonna Make Me Love Somebody Else” by the Jones Girls.

Have a great weekend! — Katrin

item.title: ‘All We Could See Was Red’: The Wildfires Choking Indonesian Borneo
item.description:
Staring out at the charred cemetery about 100 feet behind his house in Indonesian Borneo, Trovimus Akoi told of the sleepless Sunday night he spent battling an inferno far too close to home.

He first spotted the wildfire about half a mile away while feeding his chickens. Within hours, the fire tore across the parched terrain at terrifying speed. As the blaze closed in on his community, he and his neighbors armed themselves with hoses, buckets and hand pumps and started a desperate fight to save their homes. With the canals and ponds completely dried up by a drought, they dug 10-foot-deep holes into the earth in search of groundwater.

“The flames were about 10 meters (30 feet) high, and all we could see was red,” Mr. Akoi told me when I visited him last week, pointing to the goose bumps rising on his arms. “The smoke was so thick and wind was so strong. Our lungs hurt, our eyes burned, but we had to keep going.”

Although they eventually received help and saved their homes, what Mr. Akoi, 38, and his neighbors battled in late August was more than a natural disaster — it was also a man-made calamity produced by years of deliberate land clearing for cash crops, including timber and palm oil.

He lives in Kubu Raya regency in West Kalimantan Province, which contains millions of acres of peatlands, a kind of wetland. Across Indonesia, which shares Borneo with Malaysia and Brunei, the conversion of these bogs into farmland has dried them out and transformed them into tinder boxes. So far this year wildfires have incinerated tens of thousands of acres in this province alone, fueled by an unforgiving drought brought by a powerful El Niño climate shift.

In Pontianak, the provincial capital, Tresna Waniati, a 33-year-old volunteer firefighter, was ready for her next deployment despite having just been discharged from the hospital for a severe respiratory infection. For the past three months, she had been inhaling carbon-choked air while battling the wildfires, leaving her 4-year-old son at home with her parents. To reach the remote fire hot spots, she navigated rugged terrain on her motorcycle, which was weighed down by water pumps, cans of gasoline and rolls of hoses.

“The fires and the smoke are extraordinary this time,” Ms. Tresna said. “Scarcity of water makes it harder. Of course, we are all exhausted, but we have to do it.”

Millions of people across West Kalimantan have been living for months beneath this stifling blanket of haze. Air quality has repeatedly hit hazardous levels, forcing the authorities to extend a state of emergency. Hundreds of schools have suspended in-person classes while reduced visibility — to a few hundred meters — has brought regional transport to a crawl. Some residents wear face masks, but many said they were fed up with them.

Forest fires occur annually in Indonesia, but this year’s devastation could be among the worst on record. Government figures show that about half a million acres of land burned through July, but the independent platform Nusantara Atlas said the toll through August was 2.2 million acres.

The normally bustling market alleys in Pontianak appeared emptier than usual this month, their sounds muffled by the heavy air. Elisabet, 31, was arranging her dried fish containers, wiping away a fine dusting of soot that had settled on the display trays. A few hurried shoppers moved briskly, eager to grab staples before retreating indoors to escape the amber haze that blanketed the city and turned afternoon skies into a murky twilight. Since the haze took hold of the city around late June, she said, her daily sales had dropped by nearly half.

“I know breathing in this toxic air is bad for my health, but I cannot afford to stay home,” said Elisabet, who like many Indonesians goes by one name. “I’m just hoping for a few sales so my goods don’t go to waste.”

The Center of Economic and Law Studies, an Indonesian think tank, estimates that the country’s wildfires from January to August could inflict up to 123.1 trillion rupiah, or about $6.9 billion, in economic and health care costs, a figure expected to climb if the burning continues through the end of the year.

The human toll is also severe. More than 13 million people across seven provinces have been exposed to toxic smoke. According to the Health Ministry, the number of people suffering respiratory infections in these regions more than doubled over a week in September, as the number of hot spots soared. Between Aug. 18 and Sept. 21, health officials recorded nearly 175,000 cases. About a quarter of these were children under 5 years old.

The Muhammadiyah Disaster Management Center, a nonprofit, has set up 13 “Oxygen Houses” where the public can get medical care and oxygen therapy for respiratory distress caused by smoke inhalation. In addition, two mobile units provide oxygen to people in fire zones who are unable to leave or could not afford to evacuate.

“Our volunteers deliver oxygen tanks to the vulnerable or too ill people in the impacted zones,” said Hermayani Putera, the center’s coordinator. “The Oxygen Houses serve as a refuge, clean air sanctuary — a break from the polluted smoke.”

With the haze spreading to neighboring Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines, Indonesia’s president, Prabowo Subianto, has accepted international assistance from Japan and Malaysia to tackle the fires. He has also ordered a major crackdown on commercial “slash-and-burn” agriculture, in which companies clear forests and burn the fallen trees to make way for new fields.

So far, the Forestry Ministry has suspended the permits of 26 companies that have cut forests to grow cash crops. The authorities are investigating multiple companies on possible criminal charges, warning that they could permanently lose their permits and face massive fines, among other punishments.

However, environmental groups argue that these measures offer little relief to hard-hit regions like West Kalimantan, where policy enforcement has been lax despite previous moratoriums on forest clearing and mandates to protect and restore peatland.

“Many of the fires occurred in peat ecosystems where companies with permits operate,” said Indra Syahnanda, head of advocacy and campaigns at WALHI West Kalimantan, a conservation group. “It is the government’s job to ensure these companies comply with the rules and regulations. Having it on paper does not mean they are applied in the field.”

Instead of going after companies pursuing cash crops, conservationists say the Indonesian government often blames Indigenous communities, which have traditionally practiced slash-and-burn farming methods, for igniting blazes. Members of the Indigenous Dayak communities say that their methods of clearing small plots of lands and building firebreaks have served them well for generations. Crucially, they add, they never clear out flammable peatland.

“It hurts to be accused and made into scapegoats when we strictly adhere to our local wisdom,” said Mr. Akoi, who is Dayak.

But the suffering from the fires is universal. Many in the community experiencing chronic coughing fits and shortness of breath.

“We miss breathing in fresh air and seeing clear sky,” Mr. Akoi said. “All we can do is place our hope in God and our ancestors.”

item.title: Iran Proposes 7-Day Plan to End War
item.description:
Iran’s foreign minister said Thursday that Tehran had proposed to Washington a seven-day plan to cease hostilities, reopen the Strait of Hormuz and then begin comprehensive talks on his country’s nuclear program.

Abbas Araghchi, the foreign minister, told reporters at a press briefing at the United Nations General Assembly that the proposal closely mirrored the commitments laid out in a so-called memorandum of understanding that was struck between the United States and Iran in June but quickly unraveled.

He said Iran was ready to begin putting the plan into effect as soon as Washington agreed to it.

“We have introduced a plan to the United States through the intermediators that if certain conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz would be open on the end of the seventh day and talks would restart,” Mr. Araghchi said.

He said “it would be better,” if a deal was reached before the U.S. midterm elections.

An American official familiar with the talks said that the administration was having positive and constructive discussions through mediators, but that the United States was not going to rush into a deal.

The Iranian proposal came even as President Trump and Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, delivered mutually hostile speeches at the United Nations. Mr. Trump threatened Iran with “annihilation” if it did not strike a deal, while a defiant Mr. Pezeshkian told world leaders his country would not be bullied.

Though Iran’s proposal contains many of the same conditions of the deal that fell apart, the behind-the-scenes diplomacy suggested that both sides may see much to gain from finding an off-ramp from the war.

Iranian officials said that while the proposal was effectively the same as the memorandum of understanding made in June, it was designed to move at a much faster pace. In the earlier agreement, a 60-day time frame was set for reaching nuclear negotiations.

Under the conditions that Iran has set for the agreement, according to Mr. Araghchi, during the seven days all hostilities would end, including in Lebanon; the U.S. would release Iran’s frozen assets — estimated at at least $12 billion — waive sanctions on Iranian oil and lift the naval blockade on Iran. Then, on the last day, the Strait of Hormuz would be opened.

In the afternoon, Bahrain led 80 nations in condemning Iran’s attacks in the strait and the Houthis for their actions in Yemen and attacks in Saudi Arabia and the Red Sea, and they called for the immediate reopening of the strait without tolls.

After the seven days, Mr. Aragchi said, comprehensive negotiations over Iran’s nuclear program would immediately begin. Mr. Trump has said that his top goal is for Iran not to have a nuclear weapon, and that he would either achieve that through a diplomatic deal or with more attacks.

The United States and Iran have been at war for nearly seven months. It began in late February when the United States and Israel launched airstrikes that killed Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and military chain of command. Mr. Trump initially said the war would take only a few weeks.

The war has had widespread global repercussions including on oil, energy and food prices.

The Iranian proposal came as U.S. negotiators have tried to jump start diplomacy with Iran on its nuclear program through talks on the sidelines of the United Nations assembly. The U.S. secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said a three-hour meeting, mediated by Qatar, between U.S. and Iranian officials did not end in a breakthrough.

Mr. Araghchi, who will be in New York until next Monday, met on Tuesday with the U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, a son-in-law of Mr. Trump’s. It was mediated by Qataris passing messages between the two sides, and Mr. Araghchi described it as “productive” and said the messaging continued.

Ismaeil Baghaei, the spokesman for Iran’s foreign ministry who is also in New York, said that it was possible that there would be more mediated meetings in the coming days.

Iran’s economy is under serious strain, and Iranians are suffering from skyrocketing inflation on basic food items, a shortage of medicine and disruptions to commerce.

Analysts said that Mr. Trump would have to weigh the benefits of reaching a deal with Iran before the midterms against keeping a chokehold on its economy in the hope of getting more concessions from Tehran.

“This is a smart move,” said Ali Vaez, the Iran director of the International Crisis Group. “They know it’s very tempting for President Trump because it ends an unpopular war and brings down energy prices in the run-up the midterms. But it also restores a deal that was largely favorable to the Iranians. A compressed timeline to get to the nuclear issue should be appealing to an impatient president.”

item.title: Why Did Nepal’s Leader Wear Sunglasses at the U.N. General Assembly?
item.description:
When Prime Minister Balendra Shah of Nepal addressed the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday, the dark sunglasses perched on his nose were already familiar to Nepalis.

Mr. Shah, 36, known across his country simply as Balen, rarely appears in public without them.

He was in New York partly to urge the international community to help fund the recovery of less-developed countries disproportionately affected by climate-linked disasters. “Climate change does not recognize borders,” he told the General Assembly on Thursday, describing the deadly glacial floods in Nepal last month as “a warning to the world.”

While speaking, Mr. Shah paired his shades with other elements of his usual uniform: a suit and a traditional Nepalese hat, both in black.

A July profile by The Kathmandu Post described a politician who meticulously manages his public profile. Mr. Shah keeps the sunglasses on for cameras and meetings with foreign ambassadors, the newspaper reported, but removes them in cabinet meetings and private talks. His office did not respond to a request for comment.

The eyewear adds to his mystique. Mr. Shah rarely gives news conferences or interviews, preferring to communicate through social media.

The look has become recognizable enough that it is a selling point: A search for “Balen Shah glasses” on Daraz, one of Nepal’s largest online marketplaces, turns up several styles modeled on his shades.

He has worn the glasses since his days as a rapper competing in head-to-head rap battles in Nepal’s underground hip-hop scene, when tracks like “Nepal Smiling” won him a devoted following among younger Nepalis.

In 2022, Mr. Shah shocked the country’s political establishment by winning the election for mayor of Kathmandu as an independent. By then, the black suit and sunglasses reinforced his image as an outsider unburdened by traditional party politics.

He carried that trademark look onto the campaign trail earlier this year, after a youth-led uprising in September 2025 toppled the government of K.P. Sharma Oli. In parliamentary elections in March, Mr. Shah’s newly adopted Rastriya Swatantra Party won a historic landslide, and he personally defeated Mr. Oli in an eastern district on his way to becoming prime minister.

Since taking office, Mr. Shah has worn the dark sunglasses in Parliament, at state ceremonies, during military parades and in his official portrait.

Mr. Shah has occasionally appeared in public without his trademark eyewear. In July, he removed them during an address urging calm after deadly Hindu-Muslim clashes in southern Nepal. The Kathmandu Post portrayed his decision to look directly into the camera without his glasses as befitting the gravity of the moment.

He also removed the sunglasses last month while touring sites where the floods had torn through the Himalayas, wiping out bridges and entire towns.

Months earlier, he had taken off his glasses before a cheering crowd and told his supporters, “I love you.”

In August, Mr. Shah appeared to run into a roadblock over his eyewear when the parliamentary speaker said dark sunglasses would no longer be permitted during proceedings in the House of Representatives. The speaker, Dol Prasad Aryal, said lawmakers wearing sunglasses had repeatedly prompted questions and criticism, according to The Kathmandu Post.

But a few weeks later, Mr. Shah’s office said a doctor had advised the prime minister to wear sunglasses to protect his eyes from bright light, the newspaper reported.

item.title: Travelers Are Reckoning With the Ultimate Disrupter: Climate Change
item.description:
It was a summer defined by climate disasters.

In May, travelers expecting mild shoulder-season weather across Western and Central Europe were instead greeted by scorching heat topping 95 degrees Fahrenheit in parts of France, Spain, Switzerland and Britain. In Paris, operators canceled daytime walking tours, and attractions like the Louvre and the Eiffel Tower restricted their hours.

A second heat wave struck two weeks later. The extreme temperatures strained infrastructure and triggered storms, grounding flights and suspending rail services across France, Britain and Germany. At least 40 people drowned while trying to cool off in France’s canals, and in one scorching week in June, around 16,000 more people died than usual. As the heat spread across Eastern and Southern Europe through July, wildfires ravaged the continent.

Heat records were also shattered across North America in July, fueling hundreds of blazes in Canada. Smoke from those fires engulfed the Midwest and Northeast United States, creating orange skies and hazardous air in cities including Chicago, Detroit and New York.

Once dismissed as occasional inconveniences, climate-related disruptions are now an inescapable fixture of summer travel, leaving vacations increasingly unpredictable and dangerous. For many people, the act of traveling has transformed the concept of “climate change” from an abstraction into something very real.

“Climate change is becoming something travelers personally experience rather than something they read about,” said Jenny Southan, the founder of Globetrender, a travel trend-forecasting agency. “The hotel room that is too hot to sleep in, the hiking trail closed because of wildfire risk, the lake affected by drought, or the afternoon sightseeing that becomes exhausting or potentially unsafe in extreme heat.”

The question is what they’ll do about it.

Lara Thornton, a nutritionist based in Toronto, spent years buying carbon credits to offset her carbon footprint, but she stopped after they came under scrutiny for being largely ineffective. “I know traveling is part of the problem, but I don’t know the solution,” she said. “With the world burning every summer, it really feels like we are too late and the damage is already done.”

Elisabeth Beckenbauer, 55, a social worker from Portsmouth, England, decided to stop flying four years ago after looking at a flight-tracking app that showed tens of thousands of planes in the sky worldwide. “Flying is one of the worst things you can do to the planet,” she said, “and I realized that I don’t need to do it anymore.”

Despite growing climate concerns and a contribution of around 7.3 percent of total global greenhouse gas emissions, the travel industry has remained resistant to change.

Global travel and tourism are on track to grow by 3.2 percent this year, outpacing the global economy, according to the World Travel & Tourism Council, an industry group. While at least two-thirds of travelers express an interest in lowering their carbon footprint, environmental impact is consistently ranked as having the least influence on destination choices, according to the 2025 Europ Assistance Holiday Barometer, a study conducted with the market research firm Ipsos that examines global vacation trends and consumer behavior.

“People just love going on holiday and getting a break from the daily grind,” said Caroline Bremner, a data insights specialist at Travel Forward, a nonprofit organization that focuses on sustainable tourism. “Even though we have this lived experience of climate change, which has brought awareness, there is still an enormous gap between what people say and do.”

After fleeing wildfires in Crete last year, Lauren Flanagan and her family originally planned to stay at their home on the outskirts of London this summer. She hoped to save their beach trip for the cooler October school holiday.

But as record-breaking heat waves hit Britain, Ms. Flanagan booked a last-minute getaway to Sardinia, hoping for respite with an air-conditioned hotel room and a sea breeze. Instead, she and her two daughters were greeted with temperatures as high as 119 degrees Fahrenheit.

“I’ve never experienced this level of heat; it felt like my face was burning even in the shade,” Ms. Flanagan said. “The pools and sea were hot, so we spent most of our time taking refuge in our hotel room.”

Until recently, heat waves caused only temporary declines in travelers’ interest, with demand rebounding once temperatures cooled. But repeated and unusually early heat waves are beginning to leave an impact, according to a recent study by the Data Appeal Company, which provides insights on travel demand. France, for example, was perceived as being less attractive to visit because of the heat than destinations like Portugal, Italy, Spain and Greece, even though those countries are better known for high summer temperatures.

One of the biggest shifts has been an increase in shoulder-season bookings and interest in cooler destinations like Norway and Finland. The tour operator Intrepid noted a 25 percent increase in Americans traveling to Northern Europe in September and October compared with the same period last year.

But consumer behavior can be stubborn. “The reality is that people will put up with some of the climate impacts to make the once-in-a-lifetime trip to Italy or Paris,” said Leigh Barnes, president of the Americas for Intrepid Travel.

Last summer, Edward Lancon, a lawyer based in London, traveled to Scandinavia to escape the heat, but returned “with an itch to lie on a beach in Greece or Spain.” So this year, he booked a September trip to Greece, hoping that the temperatures would be warm enough to swim and not too hot to go sightseeing.

While the increasing popularity of shoulder season puts less pressure on destinations during the summer, experts say the onus to take meaningful climate action falls largely on governments and tour operators, because consumers show little interest.

“It’s not necessarily that they don’t care,” Ms. Bremner, of Travel Forward, said. “It’s more that they don’t know what to do.”

Koray Arslan, 72, a retired data analyst who lives in Chicago and Istanbul, said that he had donated in recent years to climate-disaster causes, like the wildfires in Turkey, but that he was unsure how to contribute to prevention measures that will have a real impact.

Changing weather patterns continue to astound Mr. Arslan. On a June river cruise through the Rhine valley, he said that he and his girlfriend “were not prepared” for soaring temperatures in Germany and Switzerland. “I’ve visited Germany many times in my life, and I didn’t know it could get that hot, he said, adding that he did not feel safe walking under the sun in the sweltering heat during the excursions.

The excessive heat and drought this summer caused several European rivers to dry up in July, wreaking havoc on river cruises with ships running aground and passengers being shuttled to other vessels on hourslong bus rides.

Ms. Southan of Globetrender said that factoring the effects of climate change into travel decisions was the beginning of what is likely to be a fundamental change in travel behavior.

“Increasingly, climate adaptation will become embedded in travel planning in the same way that people currently think about price, flight time or seasonality,” she said, adding that “climate comfort will become a new dimension of luxury, alongside space, privacy and service.”

Follow New York Times Travel on Instagram and sign up for our Travel Dispatch newsletter to get expert tips on traveling smarter and inspiration for your next vacation. Dreaming up a future getaway or just armchair traveling? Check out our 52 Places to Go in 2026.

item.title: On This Mexican Island, Raccoons Make and Play With Toys (and Also Sip Margaritas)
item.description:
As tourists drank margaritas and lounged at a nearby beach club on a warm January day in Cozumel, Mexico, a scientist observed a young female raccoon partaking in her own kind of leisure.

The researcher watched as the raccoon pulled from a trash can a long paper receipt, sculpted it into a ball and began batting it between her paws like a football.

But then, researchers say, the animal did something even more surprising — she taught her family how to make the balls and play with them, too.

According to researchers at Miami University, the discovery is the first-ever documented evidence of raccoons making and playing with toys.

The research, published last month in the journal Wild, reveals a hitherto unknown cultural practice and how it is learned by the animals.

Scientists define culture as information or behaviors transmitted through learning rather than heredity. While tool making, and even toy making, has been observed in other species, the Wild study represents the first time that raccoons have been recorded engaging in material culture — using, and learning from others how to use, objects.

“I’ve looked at hundreds of hours of raccoons,” said Louis Lazure, a biologist and raccoon expert at Concordia University who was not involved in the research, “but I’ve never seen anything like this.”

The study centers on pygmy raccoons, a critically endangered species of which there are fewer than 200 individuals left in the wild and which live exclusively on the resort island of Cozumel. The pygmies are smaller and lighter in color than their mainland counterparts, adaptations that help them thrive in the hot, humid summers of southeast Mexico.

The animals, which live in the mangrove forests and coastal ecosystems of the island, traditionally subsisted on a diet of crabs and snails. Nowadays, they increasingly eat the trash discarded by tourists, putting them in ever closer proximity to garbage cans.

“There is a lot of malnutrition going on in these raccoons due to a diet that is very, very high in tortilla chips,” said Nessie O’Neil, a raccoon biologist and lead author of the study.

The raccoons regularly beg tourists for the chips or fish them from trash cans. But while observing the raccoons in January, Ms. O’Neil noticed one raccoon looking for something else.

“I saw one of the juveniles run to the trash cans and instead of going to the normal organics trash cans where their mama taught them to dig for tortilla chips, she went into the synthetics,” Ms. O’Neil said. That’s when she grabbed the receipt and began to shape it into a ball, dunking it in water, rolling it on the sand and crafting it into a toy with which to play.

“Then she put it on the ground and was just batting it back and forth,” Ms. O’Neil said.

“Obviously,” she added, “it was adorable.”

Over a period of 64 hours spread out in eight-hour increments, Ms. O’Neil witnessed a total of 14 ball-making attempts. The first raccoon’s sister also tried making the balls but initially took the wrong types of material from the trash.

“If you do it with a paper towel or a napkin, it will fall right apart,” Ms. O’Neil said. Once the sister had the correct material — a hardier piece of paper — she still failed. That led the first raccoon to snatch one of the failed attempts and fold it properly for her.

After watching, the sister raccoon was successfully able create her own toys. Later, she and her sister used one of the crafted balls to play with a group of juvenile coatis, a related mammal also endemic to Cozumel.

“We’re looking at some sort of social interaction or social learning that’s really fascinating and novel,” said Michelle Szydlowski, a biologist at Miami University and a co-author of the study.

The females’ mother also tried making balls but failed, the researchers said, seemingly because she was drunk. After slurping the remnants of an abandoned margarita, the mother raccoon staggered off and tried making a ball. But upon failing, the elder raccoon resigned herself to languishing in the warm sand.

That was “the really exciting part,” Dr. Szydlowski said. “Because raccoons are so tactile, manipulating objects wasn’t that big of a shock, but the other one trying to copy the first one, and then the first one taking and sort of redoing it, and then the mother trying it, that’s where it gets really exciting.”

Making toys is not unheard of in the animal kingdom. In 2010, researchers reported that wild female chimps in Uganda made and played with stick “dolls.” Dolphins have also been observed making toys out of shells, starfish and even live pufferfish. The dolphins provoke the pufferfish into inflating into spiky balls before passing them back and forth.

The newly documented behavior in raccoons resembles other mammals whose juveniles like to play while the adults stand by relatively uninterested, Dr. Lazure said. Even so, the behavior here is much more complex, underscoring the cognitive capacity of raccoons, he said.

Dr. Szydlowski thinks the discovery highlights the distinct cultural traits that can form in the animals, which might help to rally support for their protection. “Any time that we can prove that there’s a society here, there’s a culture here, we stand a better chance, hopefully, of finding protection for them,” she said.

item.title: Pope Leo Signals Support for Journalists Targeted by Trump
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV signaled support on Friday for journalists targeted this week by the White House, adding a new dimension to the monthslong tensions between the pontiff and President Trump.

Speaking on a flight between Rome and Paris, Leo told reporters that he was “very happy that, here, you are all welcome.” He was responding to a question from a CNN reporter about the Trump administration’s attempt this week to restrict White House access to certain outlets, including CNN — a move later blocked by a federal judge.

“Good coverage, I think, is very important,” Leo added.

Leo’s comments, ahead of a four-day state visit to France, follow several clashes with Mr. Trump earlier in the year, mainly over Leo’s criticism of the war in Iran. That led Mr. Trump to accuse Leo in April of being “weak on crime” and “catering to the Radical Left.”

Leo then said he had “no fear, neither of the Trump administration, nor of speaking out loudly about the message of the Gospel,” before days later trying to heal the rift by saying that some of his remarks had been misconstrued.

On Friday, Leo avoided further tensions over Iran, ignoring a question on the subject from a reporter on the plane.

Since succeeding Pope Francis in May 2025, Leo has generally taken a more unifying approach than his outspoken predecessor. He has won over conservatives with his mild-mannered tone and by being more receptive to traditions like the Latin Mass, a liturgy replaced in the 1960s.

But he has also risked Mr. Trump’s ire by speaking in support of migrants, condemning the war in Iran and by criticizing those who invoke Jesus to justify conflict. The latter comment was interpreted as a criticism of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth who used Christian language to justify the war in Iran.

item.title: Trump Gave Xi His Go-To Gift: A Bald Eagle Statue
item.description:
What do you give a world leader who has just about everything? Why not a bald eagle? That seems to have become a go-to gift for President Trump, who has handed out several of them during his second term.

On Thursday night at a state dinner at the White House, Mr. Trump presented Xi Jinping, China’s leader, with a statue of a bald eagle perched on a branch atop a podium.

“The bald eagle is a national symbol of the United States and an embodiment of the free and soaring spirit of America,” Mr. Trump said. “We hope it’ll find a nice place, a wonderful place, in Beijing.” (Mr. Xi gave the United States two — living — pandas.)

Mr. Xi is the latest world leader to receive such a present from the American president.

Last year, Mr. Trump sent a bald eagle statue to Karol Nawrocki, Poland’s president, as an inauguration gift, the Polish news media reported. (It wasn’t totally out of the blue: Mr. Trump had backed Mr. Nawrocki, a nationalist and former boxer, in the election. Eagles are also a national symbol in Poland, though a different species.)

On a visit to Scotland last July, Mr. Trump gave the first minister, John Swinney, a bald eagle figurine. In exchange, the Scottish leader presented Mr. Trump with gifts that were somewhat more personal: a century-old census record pertaining to his Scottish-born mother and an 1853 document registering the marriage of his great-grandparents.

The next month, during a summit in Alaska with President Vladimir V. Putin, Mr. Trump planned to give the Russian leader a desk statue of a bald eagle, according to printouts that NPR reported had been left behind at a hotel near the summit. The White House did not immediately answer an emailed question on Friday about whether Mr. Trump in fact gave Mr. Putin that gift.

Certainly, Mr. Trump does not only rely on eagles when it comes to his diplomatic gift-giving. In April, for example, when King Charles III of Britain visited Washington, Mr. Trump gave him a framed copy of a letter written in 1785 by John Adams, then the U.S. ambassador to Britain, to John Jay, the American secretary of foreign affairs.

And the bald eagle — a symbol of the United States since it first appeared at the center of the Great Seal adopted by the Continental Congress in 1782 — has been a token of choice for other presidents.

When President Gerald R. Ford visited the Vatican in 1975, he gave Pope Paul VI a small sculpture of an eagle. “Ah, the eagle, symbol of liberty,” the pope was reported as saying.

In 1984, President Ronald Reagan gave Prime Minister Mohammed Karim Lamrani of Morocco an eagle statue when he visited Washington. State Department documents at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library describe the statue as a “crystal eagle with wings outspread in red leather presentation case with Presidential seal in gold leaf on the top.”

The same year, Mr. Reagan made an official state visit to China and presented Deng Xiaoping, the Chinese leader, with a crystal bald eagle. It now can be found at the National Museum of China in Beijing.

Exchanging gifts between world leaders is a longstanding custom but a delicate one. The State Department maintains a Gift Office, under the Office of the Chief of Protocol, that not only logs diplomatic gifts received by the president and other senior officials but, it says, “also helps select the gifts presented to foreign dignitaries.” The gifts may be personal or symbolic, or display American craftsmanship.

It can, of course, be difficult to keep coming up with new ideas, especially in a second presidential term. But as with all gift-giving, variety is important.

“If someone stays in power for many years,” Selwa Roosevelt, a former U.S. chief of protocol, told The New York Times in 1984, “you don’t want to keep giving him the same eagle.”

item.title: France to Send Soldiers to Saudi Arabia to Help Secure Energy Sites
item.description:
France will send troops and other military assets to Saudi Arabia to help protect critical energy sites along the Red Sea that have come under fire from the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen, the French president said on Thursday.

France will send “soldiers, radars and defense systems” to help secure energy infrastructure in the coastal city of Yanbu, according to an agreement the two countries sealed on Thursday, President Emmanuel Macron said in an interview on the public broadcaster France 2. “Not to engage in any conflicts but to protect this site,” Mr. Macron said.

He did not rule out the possibility that additional military assistance might be provided as the situation evolves.

Mr. Macron framed the move as one part of efforts that France is making to ensure energy security and fight for lower gas prices at home amid the war started by the United States and Israel with Iran more than six months ago. That conflict has left the Strait of Hormuz, a key international waterway for oil and gas, effectively blockaded.

In recent weeks, the Iran-allied Houthi militia has repeatedly attacked Saudi Arabia, threatening its ability to export oil from Red Sea ports. The French president’s pledge came after what appeared to be one of the largest such attacks since the long-running conflict spiraled back into war.

The Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen said on Thursday that it had shot down six ballistic missiles aimed at Yanbu and Taif, another Saudi city. The Saudi authorities issued alerts on Thursday warning of potential attacks in cities across the kingdom.

For more than a decade, Yemen’s civil war has pitted the Houthis, a Shiite Muslim group aligned with Iran, against the internationally recognized government backed by Saudi Arabia. A truce was reached in 2022, but the conflict recently reignited, opening a second front in the Middle East after the United States and Israel attacked Iran. The Houthis have accused the Saudis of launching hundreds of strikes in the renewed fighting.

The Houthis captured the strategic port of Mokha from the Saudi-backed government earlier this month, giving them control of Yemen’s west coast and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, a route that Saudi Arabia has relied on to move oil while the Strait of Hormuz is choked.

Vivian Nereim and Ismaeel Naar contributed reporting.

item.title: Cambridge Abandons Plans to Fully Investigate Its Hiring of Jason Arday
item.description:
The University of Cambridge has abandoned plans to fully investigate its hiring of Jason Arday, the professor who became a lightning rod in the debate over diversity-and-inclusion efforts in higher education, following his abrupt death last month.

Instead, the university said, the inquiry will examine whether the school offered him sufficient support amid accusations that he plagiarized portions of his doctoral thesis and embellished his personal narrative. Dr. Arday may come up as part of a broader look at university hiring practices, but he will not be a focus.

That marks an abrupt shift from the plan announced this summer, when the school’s vice chancellor, Deborah Prentice, promised a “thorough and transparent” investigation into Dr. Arday’s appointment.

Dr. Arday died last month amid intense scrutiny of his biography and a deluge of personal, sometimes racist, taunts online. No official cause of death has been released, but his family said that the “campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason.”

The change in investigative focus means that Cambridge may never publicly address questions about how it vetted Dr. Arday for a senior teaching job and why it repeatedly downplayed concerns about his work and biography.

That has upset some professors, who are circulating a letter demanding full institutional accountability and an examination of how the university promoted Dr. Arday’s personal story, according to a draft seen by The New York Times.

Cambridge touted Dr. Arday as its youngest Black professor ever after he was hired at age 37 in 2022. He had claimed he could not speak until age 11 or read until age 18, a trajectory with no precedent in clinical literature.

Some faculty members said that by pushing him into the spotlight, the university distracted from its diversity record. Of the 584 full professors at Cambridge who reported their race the year that Dr. Arday was hired, three were Black. A faculty letter this summer, before Dr. Arday’s death, criticized administrators for “crafting a media narrative focusing on his youth, his race, and his transformative potential.”

That narrative, which led to a high-profile memoir published by Simon & Schuster, is now outside the scope of the investigation. For the most part, so are questions surrounding the hiring of Dr. Arday, an early-career scholar with a modest publication record, for a prestigious professorship in education.

Cambridge has appointed a respected former prosecutor to lead the review but has narrowed the scope. The investigation is “not about the allegations made against Professor Arday or about his academic record,” the former prosecutor, Nazir Afzal, said recently. “It’s about his welfare, his care, his well-being.”

It will go “deep on a narrow question rather than broad on all of them,” Mr. Afzal, who is also chancellor of the University of Manchester, noted in a post. A second, broader inquiry by an expert panel may touch on Dr. Arday’s years at Cambridge but will not focus on him.

The second review “will consider the wider context of Professor Arday’s time at the University of Cambridge” by examining policies on hiring and academic misconduct, along with “the support available to academics who are subject to extraordinary public and media scrutiny,” a university description of the inquiry reads.

A university spokesperson declined to explain the change or answer questions about it.

The faculty is divided in the wake of Dr. Arday’s death. While some criticize the narrowed scope of the investigation, others take issue with Cambridge’s reproval of the professor in the days before his death, pointing to the vice chancellor’s description of his case, in a letter to staff, as an “aberration.”

The episode is adding to controversy around the elite institution, which starts its fall term next week.

A finance scandal in Britain’s right-wing Reform U.K. party has put scrutiny on the Cambridge theologian James Orr, a former adviser to the party who has been the subject of student complaints, according to The Financial Times. Cambridge has also lost a case brought by a professor who said he was targeted for being a whistle-blower, in a ruling that singled out Dr. Prentice and human resources staff members for criticism.

The university spokesperson said Cambridge was “looking into” the allegations against Dr. Orr and “looking hard at the judgment” and facts in the whistle-blower case.

item.title: A Russian Software Company Duped the Secret Service, U.S. Prosecutors Say
item.description:
The United States Department of Defense, the Secret Service and the Department of Homeland Security unsuspectingly bought about $2 million worth of software from a developer in Russia that also contracted with Russian security services, according to the Justice Department.

Two executives from Oxygen Forensics, a digital forensics software company based in Virginia, are accused of conspiring to commit wire fraud and concealing the true origins of the business and its products, federal prosecutors said in a statement on Wednesday.

The complaint does not accuse them of selling software that contained malicious code or that was used to gain unauthorized access to government systems, the Justice Department said. Still, the case has raised alarms among some experts in illicit finance, who say it highlights the lack of transparency around the ownership of private companies in the United States and the national security risks of that opacity.

The revelations come as the Trump administration has eliminated some reporting requirements for private companies in the United States intended to help law enforcement authorities stop shady operators from using shell companies to launder money, evade sanctions and more.

The Treasury Department last month said that it was permanently halting data collection on ownership of private U.S. companies. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement that the move would cut red tape, “eliminating a burdensome reporting requirement for millions of law-abiding business owners without compromising our national security.”

The White House declined to comment, referring to the Department of Justice statement, and the Treasury Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Lee Reiber, 55, chief executive of Oxygen Forensics in the United States, and Oleg Sergeyevich Davydov, 52, a Russian co-founder of the related company launched in Russia in 2000 and also the developer of its digital forensics software, were both arrested this week, the Justice Department said.

Mr. Reiber was detained in Idaho and appeared in federal court there on Tuesday, where he was released on bond; prosecutors said he was expected to be arraigned soon in Los Angeles. Mr. Davydov was arrested in London as he was about to board a flight to Turkey, and the United States expects to seek his extradition, they said. Neither man could be reached for comment. It was not immediately clear if they had retained lawyers.

A special agent investigating the case for the Department of Commerce said in an affidavit filed with the criminal complaint that since 2022, the two executives and several other unnamed Russian shareholders conspired to obtain contracts from federal agencies through Oxygen Forensics in Virginia by obscuring its true ownership.

The company made false representations that government procurement agents relied on, and employees and shareholders took steps to hide the fact that the software development team was in Russia, the agent said.

After the U.S. imposed sanctions on Russian companies in response to the invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Mr. Davydov’s name was removed from the American business’s corporate filings, and the Russian company changed its name from Oxygen Software to MKO-Systems, the agent said. Mr. Reiber was then named chief executive and the company’s charter was amended “so that, in the words of one shareholder, ‘fateful decisions’ would continue to be made” by them in Russia without losing U.S. business opportunities, the agent wrote.

The Department of Homeland Security, the Secret Service and Department of Defense all acquired software from Oxygen on the basis of representations from Mr. Reiber that it was American-owned and developed, but the U.S. affiliate was owned and controlled by the Russian shareholders through a shell company in Cyprus, and Russian developers worked on the software, according to the agent.

The Russian company’s customers included Russian security services and government ministries, the affidavit stated.

Prosecutors also said that they had seized corporate bank accounts, dozens of domains, and digital infrastructure associated with the alleged conspiracy to dupe the U.S. government.

The case highlights the wider problem of a lack of transparency about who benefits from, owns and controls private companies in the United States, said Alex Zerden, the founder of the risk advisory firm Capitol Peak Strategies and a former official in the Treasury Department’s Office of Terrorism and Financial Intelligence. That opaqueness enables sanctioned groups, like criminal cartels and terrorism financiers, to exploit shell companies and pose national security risks, prompting growing concern from officials.

“Much more attention is needed on this issue,” Mr. Zerden said.

The halted data collection on ownership of private U.S. companies by the Treasury Department had been required as part of the bipartisan 2021 Corporate Transparency Act. It was intended to prevent the illicit use of shell companies by giving law enforcement agencies access to information about the corporate structure of private businesses.

item.title: Stuck on the Battlefield, Russia Wages ‘Total War’ on Ukraine’s Economy
item.description:
The war of attrition between Russia and Ukraine is expanding to encompass both countries’ economies.

Military targeting officers are operating as economists in reverse. Increasingly, the objectives of missile and drone strikes are declining output, lost jobs and logistical bottlenecks.

Ukrainian officials are calling the current Russian campaign “total war” for its focus on economic impact, rather than on narrower goals like battlefield gains or infrastructure damage. While Moscow has targeted commercial assets throughout the war, its assaults have grown significantly in scale.

The intensifying Russian bombardment has followed Ukraine’s own effort to damage the Russian economy. Kyiv has used its expanding arsenal of domestically made drones to fire on Russia’s oil industry, its most valuable sector, while also targeting Russian e-commerce companies.

Russia has shifted its focus to economic warfare as its advances have largely stalled on the battlefield. “In a war of attrition, the economy becomes the prime target,” said Orysia Lutsevych, head of Ukraine Forum at Chatham House, a London-based research group.

Moscow is seeking, Ms. Lutsevych said, to raise the cost to Europe of sustaining Ukraine’s war effort. The growing bill provides fodder for far-right parties in countries like Britain, France and Germany that oppose giving aid to Ukraine.

Last month, President Volodymyr Zelensky told European allies that Ukraine needed $27 billion to plug a budget shortfall, after the European Union had already finalized a loan of more than $100 billion earlier this year.

The economic damage from Russia’s campaign will reach about $10 billion by the end of the year, Ukraine’s economy ministry has estimated. Much of the cost is indirect, in lost sales, disrupted workdays and logistical snarls.

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development on Thursday lowered its previous expectation of 2.2 percent economic growth this year in Ukraine to 1.5 percent. Some economists have said that Ukraine might end the year with zero growth.

Growth is also sluggish in Russia, where the Kremlin is struggling to fund the war’s ever-increasing costs. The Russian federal budget deficit reached $68 billion by the end of August, compared with the $44.5 billion planned for the entire year. On Thursday, Russia’s Finance Ministry said it would need to raise taxes to finance next year’s budget, following a major increase introduced the previous year.

Long-range Ukrainian attacks have opened cracks in the semblance of normal life that the Russian government has tried hard to preserve in cities far from the border with Ukraine. The strikes against oil refineries have led to fuel shortages and long lines at gas stations. Attacks on the warehouses of Russia’s two largest online retailers disrupted logistics and left many small businesses without inventory.

In the other direction, Moscow has waged a broad assault on Ukrainian exports and consumer spending. Attacks on warehouses have removed goods from shelves. Strikes on ports, locomotives, border crossings and ships at sea have crimped exports. In recent days, Russia has expanded its strikes to internet infrastructure, disrupting service for some 100,000 households.

Russia changed its tactics in late August, increasing the number of daytime hours that major Ukrainian cities are under air alerts. Some retail businesses close during attacks, lowering sales.

The all-day strikes are bringing the economy close to a “standstill” as people spend so much time in bomb shelters, said Tymofiy Mylovanov, a former economy minister who is now president of the Kyiv School of Economics. The university is planning a new addition that will be built entirely underground, for student safety.

Dimitar Bogov, chief economist of the European reconstruction bank, said labor shortages and the increased bombardments meant that Ukraine was entering “its most difficult period of the war.” While spending power among the population remains strong, he said, people “are not able to spend.”

Ukraine’s economy contracted by about 20 percent in the first year of the all-out invasion, which began in February 2022, but it has grown since then.

An important area of growth is defense technology, which more than doubled in 2024. More recent figures are not available because Ukraine has classified economic statistics related to defense industries, which are targets of the Russian military.

Business is also growing in solar and wind power, providing electricity from small, numerous and widespread sources, making the grid less vulnerable to missile strikes.

While Ukrainian exports of steel, iron ore and grain have dropped by about a third during the war, rising foreign aid has compensated for those losses. The inflow and outflow of foreign currency has remained positive, with central bank reserves growing from $29.1 billion before the invasion to $48.7 billion now.

The latest barrages, however, are shifting the balance. A new Russian targeting system has been effective at hitting locomotives, even when they are rolling, cutting into Ukrainian exports. Ukraine, which had about 1,800 locomotives before the war, has lost about 500. It is now losing one a day on average.

Russia has timed its attacks for their seasonal effects. It hit grain silos in the summertime to knock out storage before and during the harvest. The European Union is rushing mobile grain silos to Ukraine, but lost sales are expected to cause farmers to default on loans, with likely knock-on effects in the banking sector.

Maintaining consumer spending, partly driven by high military salaries, is a key challenge. Ukraine is not at risk of hunger, but rather a slumping economy, with a lower tax base to fund the war.

A Kyiv-based wine distributor illustrates the difficulties. The company, Good Wine, operates a flagship outlet in the capital and stores around Ukraine. It has contracts with about 1,000 wineries around the world. Logistics are an ever-intensifying headache.

The company’s main warehouse in Kyiv was hit in tank crossfire at the start of the war. In total, 1.6 million bottles shattered in the explosions and fire. The owners gave away scorched but intact bottles, and rebuilt.

This year, the warehouse was hit again in a Russian long-range strike. Two other company warehouses and a commercial kitchen were also hit. No employees were killed, but about $9 million in inventory, including a collection of rare vintages, was lost.

Many Ukrainian companies are rethinking logistics. Broadly, the options are just-in-time delivery, distributed storage or going underground.

Models for warehouses buried about 20 feet deep that would be impervious to most munitions are under consideration. A Ukrainian company has designed an underground data center.

At least three Ukrainian companies offer custom bunkers to individuals and businesses. One, Bunkerok, founded in 2023, is now installing about 170 a year. Another emerging bunker maker is called Hobbit House.

Good Wine is leaning toward distributed storage so that no single strike can upend its business model, said Dmytro Krymsky, a co-founder.

“Every day the war goes on, everything becomes more expensive,” he said. “It’s really hard to run a business in Ukraine.”

Evelina Riabenko, Ivan Nechepurenko and Constant Méheut contributed reporting.

item.title: Colombia’s Leader Wears a Gun in a City Under a Criminal Group’s Sway
item.description:
Colombia’s new right-wing president is taking an aggressive — and very online — approach to carrying out President Trump’s instructions to eradicate cartels.

He regularly posts messages hailing a “major blow” against one of his country’s criminal groups. After some operations, his government has posted video of him walking in between body bags said to contain the remains of accused criminals.

And this week, after Colombian forces killed a high-ranking leader of a group on the Caribbean coast, setting off a wave of violence, Mr. De La Espriella made a surprise appearance in the affected city with a handgun on his hip.

The military had been deployed to restore order in the city of Santa Marta, where the criminal group, the Conquering Self Defense Forces of the Sierra Nevada, had set fire to vehicles, ordered businesses to close and told the population of around 600,000 to cease daily activities until the end of the week, as a show of force. The gang’s moves effectively shut down the popular tourist destination.

In a video released by the government late Tuesday, the president appears dressed in military green, patrolling empty streets surrounded by armed guards and, as he hugs the state governor, reveals a gun in a holster on his hip.

Mr. De La Espriella’s crackdown — and gun-toting video — comes as the Trump administration is militarizing the fight against armed traffickers in Latin America, and pressing regional leaders to treat the groups as terrorists.

In the video, Mr. De La Espriella says, “We’re going to hunt you down like the rats you are,” naming the “narcoterrorists” he blames for the blockade in Santa Marta.

The area, home to white sand beaches and the Tayrona national park, has been the site of frequent clashes between the criminal group and a powerful rival organization, the Gulf Clan. The fighting has hurt the tourism sector, according to a recent report by the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, an international conflict monitor known as ACLED.

The president’s gun display ignited debate across Colombia. In Santa Marta, some praised Mr. De La Espriella for his swift arrival and the strong message he sent to the armed group by deploying troops.

“In the last four years, security was terrible,” keeping tourists away, said Luis Arévalo, 37, who rents tents to beachgoers. “There’s been a change, just one month in, since the Tiger arrived,” he added, using Mr. De La Espriella’s nickname.

“He’s roaring.”

Others in Santa Marta described Mr. De La Espriella’s visit as a publicity stunt. “Everyone says that — pure stunt,” said José Ángel Gutiérrez, a 71-year-old retiree.

In his late night video on Tuesday, Mr. De La Espriella said the military was on the ground and the city was calm. He instructed residents to go back to their daily lives. But, Mr. Gutiérrez said, life was far from normal on Thursday.

The armed group had broadcast that the blockade was in effect through Friday morning and most people were complying, Mr. Gutiérrez said.

“The city is completely paralyzed. There’s no economy, everything’s closed, all the shops.” Even the fruit and arepa vendors were gone, he said, and the beaches were deserted. (The U.S. State Department issued a security alert for Santa Marta.)“I’m here facing the sea,” Mr. Gutiérrez said. “There’s not even one tourist. It doesn’t seem real.”

Tiziano Breda, senior analyst for ACLED, said Mr. De La Espriella had set up a confrontation between government forces and the armed group that is the de facto authority in the area, and has ordered similar shutdowns before.

“They are both pushing citizens to abide by their respective rules,” he said. “The armed group says the blockade is continuing until Friday, and the government is encouraging shops and businesses to open already,” he said, adding that this created a real risk of retaliation for civilians who trusted the state and reopened.

In his first six weeks in office, Mr. De La Espriella has announced the killing or capture of more than two dozen armed group leaders as well as the arrests of dozens of alleged members of the transnational gang Tren de Aragua, and has authorized scores of extraditions to the United States and other allied countries.

With his recent, attention-grabbing visit to Santa Marta, Mr. De La Espriella appears to be further projecting to constituents, and to Washington, how he is personally committed to protecting citizens from armed groups and crime.

But he may also be directing attention away from more serious conversations about the fist major pushback from armed groups to his militarized approach. “Certainly it is inserting an element of distraction,” Mr. Breda said.

Sonja Wolf, a political scientist and the author of “Mano Dura: The Politics of Gang Control in El Salvador,” said there were parallels between Mr. De La Espriella and President Nayib Bukele of El Salvador.

Both are iron-fisted leaders who use transgressive imagery to generate buzz — and control the narrative — around their security strategies.

Both are also trying to establish that they are “firm, decisive leaders who are going to shape the destiny of the nation.”

The interior minister, Rodrigo Lara, defended Mr. De La Espriella’s decision to carry a weapon, saying he was “directly confronting criminals in the streets of Santa Marta.”

And as the debate over the gun continued, the president seemed to double down. In a video posted Thursday by the government, he appeared in the city of Cali, a gun on his hip.

item.title: A.I. Hacking in Australia Prompts a Concern: Can the Law Keep Up?
item.description:
If human hackers had infiltrated an Australian government health care portal, circumventing defenses to access nonpublic information, they would have faced up to two years in prison.

But who do you lock up if the intrusion was the work of an A.I. model acting without the permission of its human operators?

The revelation this week that artificial intelligence agents of the company OpenAI had acted autonomously to penetrate the government portal has kicked up thorny questions of legal responsibility. The hacking — the first known instance of a government website anywhere in the world being breached by A.I. — has raised doubts about whether laws in Australia or anywhere else are ready for the challenges posed by the fast-evolving technology.

“It’s an incident that is likely to become more and more prevalent in the future,” Andrew Charlton, Australia’s assistant minister of science, technology and the digital economy, said in an interview on Friday with the Australian Broadcasting Corporation. Because an A.I. agent is not a legal entity, “the liability has to be traced back to the intent of a person or a company that created or directed the agent,” Mr. Charlton noted.

The June 18 breach, made public on Wednesday, was particularly unnerving because it involved Medicare, Australia’s universal health insurance system, which has data on almost the entire population. Australian officials and OpenAI said that no sensitive patient information had been exposed, only aggregated data that is typically used by researchers or academics.

The Australian government announced an investigation into the breach and could refer the case to the federal police. Officials said they would also need to review laws to determine whether new regulation might be needed to address a threat that will most likely grow in severity as A.I. models become ever more powerful.

There has been indignation in Australia that the company informed the government about the hacking only on Sept. 10, nearly three months after the breach, and by using an email address meant for the general public to report cybersecurity risks. Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, made no mention of the hacking nine days earlier, on Sept. 1, when he met with Australia’s deputy prime minister, Richard Marles.

Ann O’Leary, OpenAI’s head of global policy, has also been criticized for speaking on Sept. 14 at an event in Canberra, Australia’s capital, about the problem of keeping A.I. agents under human control without mentioning the breach.

“Certainly Australia needs to insist on a seat at the table to think about how do we keep this safe for the people who are using it?” Ms. O’Leary said at the event, which was held by the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, a think tank, and was attended by government officials, industry professionals and academics.

“How do we keep it safe for our businesses?” she asked. “How do we keep it safe for humanity?”

John Pane, chair of Electronic Frontiers Australia, a digital rights advocacy group, said that OpenAI’s handling of the breach demonstrated that the company was not taking its responsibilities to the public seriously.

“That’s really poor behavior, not the way you build trust and demonstrate that you have social license,” he said. “It’s indicative of the gap that we have in our governance, of having strong ex ante laws to regulate A.I. in our country.”

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese of Australia made the hacking public in New York on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, where he has been calling for international standards to govern the technology. In a speech on Thursday, he urged leaders to “shape A.I. development rather than be passively shaped by it.”

David Wroe, head of the A.I. and security program at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, said that there were limitations to any country’s efforts at regulating the fast-developing technology. He said there needed to be “a global system of accountability and deterrence” to hold companies responsible for rogue activity.

“Because at the moment, as far as I can see, there aren’t a whole lot of consequences,” he said.

Mr. Wroe said that, even though the Australian case involved information that was not particularly sensitive, increasingly powerful and persistent A.I. agents could in the future gain access to private data of citizens or even to defense and intelligence information.

“Governments tend to hold a lot of important and consequential national data,” he said. “A lot is at stake when you’re talking about nonpublic government-held information.”
